prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: colorize
Deck beneath it: The book's black-and-white engravings pass through a painter's stall of interchangeable tools, and come out the other side in colour — or unchanged, if that is the choice.

Hero: a hand-tinting workshop drawn across the middle of the page. On the left, a drying line of black-and-white engravings hangs waiting — small landscapes and portraits clipped to a cord, all in grey ink. They feed one by one into a central painter's stall, drawn as an open wooden booth whose bench holds a row of five interchangeable tool caddies, each a small labeled box: one holds nothing but a plain paper sleeve, labeled copy — pass through untouched; one holds a modern brush wired to a small distant cloud, labeled openai; one holds a shallow dish of brown wash, labeled sepia; one an old tin labeled deoldify; one an empty bracket labeled your own script. The openai caddy sits open and in use, its brush touching an engraving on the easel. A note at the bench: one tool is chosen for the whole book; the default is the plain sleeve — no colour at all until it is wanted.

On the right, the same drying line continues out of the stall, the engravings now tinted in muted watercolour. One engraving on the line carries a small paper tag at its top edge reading no sky, and its upper region stays a quiet warm grey; a note beside it: a picture tagged in the ledger keeps its top from turning to blue sky.

Below the stall, two quiet details:
- lower left: an open ledger passing under the bench from the incoming side to the outgoing side, captioned — the manifest travels with the pictures; the next stage keeps the same ledger;
- lower right: one engraving hanging back on the incoming line with a small pinned slip, captioned — a picture that fails is noted and left for another pass; the line never stops.

Four brushes standing in a jar work in parallel at the easel's edge, captioned briefly: several pictures are painted at once.

One warm accent colour and a few muted tints belong to the finished engravings and the working brush; the stall, the waiting line, and the ledger stay in ink.
